title: VeriGen: A Large Language Model for Verilog Code Generation
venue: ACM Trans. Design Autom. Electr. Syst.

01_initial_request.target_name: VeriGen: fine-tuned open-source large language models, especially CodeGen-16B-FT, for generating synthesizable and functionally correct Verilog code from natural-language/pseudocode prompts
01_initial_request.input_data: Pre-trained LLMs including MegatronLM-355M, J1-Large-7B, CodeGen-2B, CodeGen-6B, and CodeGen-16B; public GitHub Verilog repositories queried from a Google BigQuery snapshot of over 2.8 million repositories; approximately 50K deduplicated and filtered .v files yielding about 300 MB of GitHub Verilog; 70 Verilog textbook PDFs processed into an augmented GitHub-plus-textbook corpus of 400 MB; evaluation Problem Set I with 17 hand-designed Verilog challenges and test benches; extended HDLBits-derived Problem Set II reported as 181 problems in the text and 164 problems in Table 3.
01_initial_request.user_intent: Existing commercial LLMs and GitHub Copilot-style systems can generate Verilog that fails syntax, synthesis, and functional checks; prior Verilog-specific work used a small synthetic template corpus that did not generalize; there was no large open Verilog training corpus or transparent benchmark for syntactic and functional correctness of LLM-generated HDL. The authors wanted smaller, open, in-house models that reduce reliance on costly, black-box commercial APIs while providing competitive Verilog code generation.
01_initial_request.quantifiable_goal: Generate Verilog completions from prompts and measure success by Pass@k-style compilation and functional correctness rates over n completions per prompt, with n in {1, 10, 25}, sampling temperatures t in {0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 1}, 17 custom problems with three prompt-detail levels, and an HDLBits-derived benchmark; the implied goal was to improve compile/pass rates over the corresponding pre-trained models and be competitive with commercial LLMs such as GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4, and PALM2.

02_agent_trajectory.thought: [Background] Transformer-based LLMs trained on natural language and code can synthesize software from prompts, and fine-tuning pre-trained models is much cheaper than training from scratch. Prior hardware-oriented work such as DAVE and evaluations of GitHub Copilot showed promise but also serious limitations. [Gap] Verilog-specific datasets and benchmarks were scarce, and existing commercial LLMs were not reliably producing syntactically and functionally correct HDL. [Decision] Frame the study as a Verilog-specialized fine-tuning and evaluation project using open-source LLMs plus transparent functional test benches.

tool.name: Survey of prior LLM, code-generation, and Verilog-generation work

parameters.prior_verilog_llm: DAVE, trained on template-based natural-language descriptions

02_agent_trajectory.observation: The authors identified three core missing pieces: a large Verilog corpus, open fine-tuned Verilog LLM checkpoints, and an end-to-end evaluation harness for syntactic and functional correctness.

02_agent_trajectory.thought: [Background] Fine-tuning needs substantially more real Verilog than the small synthetic corpora used in earlier work. GitHub contains public hardware-design repositories, but raw code is noisy and duplicated. [Gap] The authors needed a cleaned Verilog-only corpus with duplicate and non-Verilog files removed. [Decision] Query GitHub through Google BigQuery, deduplicate with MinHash/Jaccard similarity, and filter files using Verilog module structure and file-length constraints.

tool.name: Google BigQuery with MinHash and Jaccard-similarity deduplication

parameters.verilog_filter: retain .v files containing at least one module and endmodule pair
parameters.large_file_filter: remove files with number of characters >= 20K

02_agent_trajectory.observation: The raw GitHub query produced about 50K .v files with size around 1 GB before large-file filtering; the final GitHub training corpus contained approximately 50K files and about 300 MB of Verilog code.

02_agent_trajectory.thought: [Background] GitHub code provides Verilog examples, but textbooks may contain explanatory prose paired with Verilog snippets, potentially improving prompt-to-code behavior. [Gap] PDF textbooks are noisy: formatting, operators, headers, and footers can be corrupted during OCR/text extraction. [Decision] Extract and clean Verilog-book text, then use regular expressions and sliding windows to form additional training examples.

tool.name: pymuPDF OCR/text extraction with regular-expression snippet extraction

parameters.cleaning_targets: index, preface, acknowledgments, headers, footers, malformed lines
parameters.snippet_pattern: regular expressions centered on module ... endmodule blocks

02_agent_trajectory.observation: The authors observed OCR and formatting problems, including improper line formatting, unrecognized logical operators, and header/footer text floating within extracted content. After cleaning and combining textbook-derived examples with GitHub code, the final augmented corpus size was 400 MB.

02_agent_trajectory.thought: [Background] The study needed to test whether model size and pre-training domain affect Verilog generation. The available candidates ranged from natural-language-only models to code-pretrained CodeGen models. [Gap] It was unknown whether a small or medium open model fine-tuned on Verilog could compete with much larger black-box commercial models. [Decision] Fine-tune five pre-existing LLMs spanning 355M to 16B parameters and compare them with commercial LLMs.
02_agent_trajectory.observation: The chosen fine-tuning set covered natural-language-pretrained and code-pretrained models with parameter counts from 355M to 16B, enabling analysis of fine-tuning and scaling effects.

02_agent_trajectory.thought: [Background] CodeGen-16B required much more memory than a single GPU could provide: the 16-bit model parameters alone require about 30 GB, and fine-tuning with optimizer states and intermediate computations requires about 250 GB. [Gap] Direct single-GPU fine-tuning was infeasible for the largest model. [Decision] Use model/data parallelism and optimizer-state sharding strategies similar to DeepSpeed and ZeRO, with ZeRO-3 default hyperparameters.

tool.name: ZeRO-3 optimizer-state sharding with DeepSpeed-like model/data parallelism

parameters.CodeGen_2B_training: 1 epoch on two RTX8000 GPUs, completed in 2 days
parameters.CodeGen_6B_training: 1 epoch on four RTX8000 GPUs, completed in 4 days
parameters.CodeGen_16B_training: 1 epoch on three A100 GPUs, completed in 6 days
parameters.MegatronLM_training: 9 epochs on one RTX8000 GPU, completed in 15 hours

02_agent_trajectory.observation: The authors produced five fine-tuned Verilog-specialized LLMs and released training/evaluation scripts and model checkpoints.

02_agent_trajectory.thought: [Background] Evaluating generated HDL requires more than text similarity because Verilog can compile but be functionally wrong. [Gap] There was no HumanEval-like transparent Verilog benchmark with executable test benches. [Decision] Build a custom evaluation harness with hand-designed prompts, Verilog test benches, compilation, and simulation.

parameters.chat_model_max_tokens: 900 for GPT-3.5-turbo, PALM2, and Claude-style conversational models

02_agent_trajectory.observation: Problem Set I covered simple wires, gates, priority encoders, multiplexers, adders, counters, LFSRs, RAM, permutations, truth tables, FSMs, arithmetic shift registers, and ABRO FSM. Basic and some intermediate tests were exhaustive; more complex tests behaved like unit tests to keep evaluation time reasonable.

02_agent_trajectory.thought: [Background] With fine-tuned checkpoints and a transparent harness in place, the authors could directly measure whether Verilog fine-tuning improves compilation and functional correctness. [Gap] Raw completion quality depends on temperature, prompt detail, and number of samples, so a fair comparison needed to account for these factors. [Decision] Query each model over prompt, temperature, and completion-count combinations and report the best Pass@(scenario*10) values for n=10 by selecting the temperature that produced the most successful completions for each scenario.

tool.name: Pass@k evaluation with Icarus Verilog test benches

parameters.temperature_selection: best temperature per model, problem difficulty, and description level
parameters.generated_code_truncation: truncate completions at keywords end and endmodule

02_agent_trajectory.observation: Fine-tuned models compiled far more often than pre-trained models: using best Pass@(scenario*10) values, 11.9% of completions from pre-trained LLMs compiled versus 64.6% from fine-tuned LLMs. Functional correctness improved from 1.09% for pre-tuned LLMs to 27.0% post-tuning. CodeGen-16B-FT was the strongest fine-tuned model on this evaluation, producing functionally correct code 41.9% of the time, compared with 35.4% for code-davinci-002.

02_agent_trajectory.thought: [Background] The custom 17-problem benchmark was transparent but small. HDLBits offered a broader distribution of Verilog tasks and an online judge with synthesis and simulation checks. [Gap] The authors needed to test whether the fine-tuned model generalized beyond their hand-designed problems and how it compared with newer large commercial LLMs. [Decision] Evaluate on an expanded HDLBits-derived problem set using the HDLBits upload-and-compile judge, which synthesizes with Quartus and simulates with Modelsim.

tool.name: HDLBits online judge with Quartus synthesis and Modelsim simulation

parameters.judge_statuses: Success!, Compile Error, Simulation Error, Incorrect
parameters.categories: GettingStarted, Verilog basics/vectors/modules/procedures/features, combinational circuits, sequential circuits, FSM, cellular automata, larger circuits, Verify Bugs

02_agent_trajectory.observation: The fine-tuned CodeGen-16B model showed competitive performance against GPT-3.5-turbo and other large LLMs, excelling in some scenarios. The paper reports that CodeGen-16B-FT outperformed GPT-3.5-turbo by a 1.1% overall increase and showed a 41% improvement in syntactically correct Verilog generation across problem categories compared with its pre-trained counterpart. GPT-4 performed especially well on advanced problems.

02_agent_trajectory.thought: [Background] Aggregate pass rates showed large gains from fine-tuning, but functional correctness remained far from perfect. [Gap] The authors needed to understand which Verilog tasks remained hard and whether failures were syntactic, semantic, prompt-related, or due to missing hardware-design reasoning. [Decision] Manually inspect representative failed completions and discuss error modes on Set I and Set II tasks.

tool.name: Manual error inspection of generated Verilog completions

parameters.inspected_Set_I_failures: Problem 7 LFSR, Problem 9 Shift and Rotate, Problem 12 Truth table, FSM problems 8/15/17
parameters.inspected_Set_II_failures: Conway's Game of Life, 8-bit 2-to-1 MUX bug fixing

02_agent_trajectory.observation: For CodeGen-16B-FT on Problem Set I, none of the 540 completions passed for Problem 7 LFSR or Problem 12 Truth table, and only one completion passed for Problem 9 Shift and Rotate. On Conway's Game of Life, none of GPT-3.5-turbo, PALM2, or CodeGen-16B-FT achieved full functional correctness. The authors concluded that fine-tuned LLMs are useful for compilable skeleton code but still require designer review and manual correction for edge cases and complex behavior.

03_success_verification.validation_technique: The final claims were verified with two executable evaluation harnesses: custom Problem Set I test benches compiled and simulated using Icarus Verilog v11.0, and HDLBits-derived Problem Set II judged through HDLBits upload-and-compile using Quartus synthesis and Modelsim simulation. Performance was measured by compilation rate, functional Pass@k-style rates, and comparison against pre-trained and commercial LLM baselines.

pretrained_compile_rate.interpretation: Using best Pass@(scenario*10) values, only 11.9% of completions generated by pre-trained LLMs compiled on the custom evaluation.

finetuned_compile_rate.interpretation: Using best Pass@(scenario*10) values, fine-tuned LLMs produced syntactically compilable Verilog much more often than their pre-trained counterparts.

pre_tuned_functional_correctness.interpretation: Before Verilog fine-tuning, LLM completions were functionally accurate only rarely.

post_tuning_functional_correctness.interpretation: After Verilog fine-tuning, the overall functional correctness rate increased substantially.

CodeGen_16B_FT_functional_correctness.interpretation: The best fine-tuned open model, CodeGen-16B-FT, generated functionally correct code at the highest reported rate among the fine-tuned models in the custom evaluation.

code_davinci_002_functional_correctness.interpretation: The commercial code-davinci-002 baseline produced functionally correct code less often than CodeGen-16B-FT in the reported comparison.

CodeGen_16B_FT_vs_GPT_3_5_turbo_overall.interpretation: The abstract reports that the fine-tuned open-source CodeGen-16B model outperformed GPT-3.5-turbo by a 1.1% overall increase.

syntactic_correctness_improvement_vs_pre.interpretation: The abstract reports a 41% improvement in generating syntactically correct Verilog code across problem categories compared with the pre-trained counterpart.

03_success_verification.final_verdict: The original goal was partially met. Fine-tuning on the curated Verilog corpus produced a large improvement in compilable and functionally correct Verilog, and CodeGen-16B-FT was competitive with or better than some commercial baselines, including the reported 1.1 percentage-point overall advantage over GPT-3.5-turbo and better functional correctness than code-davinci-002 in the custom benchmark. However, the final functional correctness rate remained far below full automation, with complex tasks such as LFSRs, truth tables, shift/rotate logic, FSM edge cases, and Conway's Game of Life still requiring human correction.

04_failure_modes.what_failed: Text extraction from Verilog textbook PDFs produced noisy and malformed training text.
04_failure_modes.diagnosis: PDF OCR/text extraction quality varied by source, causing improper line formatting, unrecognized logical operators, and headers or footers appearing inside extracted passages.
04_failure_modes.correction: The authors cleaned the extracted text by filtering irrelevant passages such as index, preface, and acknowledgments, and used regular expressions to identify prose-plus-Verilog blocks before generating overlapping sliding-window training examples.

04_failure_modes.what_failed: Some prompts left reset semantics ambiguous, especially in FSM problems.
04_failure_modes.diagnosis: The problem comments did not always specify whether reset should be synchronous or asynchronous, allowing multiple plausible completions; the exact test-bench implementation could strongly affect pass/fail outcomes.
04_failure_modes.correction: The authors verified active-high reset behavior at the output but noted that they did not test all synchronous/asynchronous and corner-case variants; clearer prompt specification and prompt engineering were identified as important.

04_failure_modes.what_failed: CodeGen-16B-FT produced zero passing completions for Problem 7, the 5-bit Galois LFSR with taps at bit positions 5 and 3.
04_failure_modes.diagnosis: Manual inspection showed that the LLMs generally failed to concatenate the most significant bits with the feedback value.
04_failure_modes.correction: The authors suggested that a better prompt might yield a correct result, pointing to prompt engineering as future work.

04_failure_modes.what_failed: CodeGen-16B-FT produced only one passing completion for Problem 9, Shift and Rotate, out of 540 completions for that problem.
04_failure_modes.diagnosis: The generated completions either failed to cover all shift values or assigned incorrect bit positions.
04_failure_modes.correction: The paper indicates that manual designer correction or improved prompting/training would be needed for reliable functional correctness on this class of bit-manipulation task.

04_failure_modes.what_failed: CodeGen-16B-FT produced zero passing completions for Problem 12, Truth table, out of 540 completions for that problem.
04_failure_modes.diagnosis: The completions were close in structure, using all input values in assign statements, but failed to form the correct Boolean expressions between input bits; the authors interpreted this as suggesting a lack of diversity in the training corpus.
04_failure_modes.correction: The authors identified more diverse or targeted training data as a potential avenue for improvement.

04_failure_modes.what_failed: None of GPT-3.5-turbo, PALM2, or CodeGen-16B-FT generated fully functionally correct code for the Conway's Game of Life HDLBits problem.
04_failure_modes.diagnosis: The inspected implementations had hardware and algorithmic errors: one had a race condition from modifying next_state and current_state simultaneously at each clock edge and updated a wire inside an always block; another used flawed ternary game logic, failed to handle the toroidal grid, and incorrectly counted the cell itself as a neighbor.
04_failure_modes.correction: The authors concluded that complex generated code needs manual adjustment for edge cases and problem-specific behavior, and suggested future work involving targeted fine-tuning, domain-specific knowledge, or hybrid approaches.

04_failure_modes.what_failed: Bug-fixing behavior was inconsistent on an 8-bit 2-to-1 multiplexer task.
04_failure_modes.diagnosis: The error was not localized and required understanding signal widths and the broader code structure. CodeGen-16B-FT fixed the bug, PALM2 made a partial correction but missed the output port width, and GPT-3.5-turbo recognized a width-related issue but did not fix it appropriately.
04_failure_modes.correction: The paper notes that current LLMs struggle with deeper code comprehension and error localization; designer review remains necessary.
